wu: Students play 'Find Someone Who...' with a Labour Day twist: ask 3 classmates 'Do you have a job?' or 'Do you want a job?' and write names. Teacher models first with a volunteer.
wuAlt: Teacher shows 5 job flashcards (teacher, doctor, engineer, chef, driver); students stand up and say 'I am a...' for their dream job.
Teacher writes 'Work is...' on board; students brainstorm 1 word each (e.g., 'important', 'hard').
pres: Teacher presents a short dialogue about unpaid internships using flashcards (student, boss, money bag, clock). Model: 'Internships help you learn, but not getting paid is bad.' Check understanding by asking 'Is this fair?' and having students thumbs up/down.
presAlt: Teacher reads a short paragraph for/against unpaid internships; students repeat key phrases like 'It is good experience' and 'It is not fair.'
Teacher draws a simple T-chart on board; students copy and write 1 'pro' and 1 'con' with teacher guidance.
prac: Students work in pairs to complete a gap-fill worksheet with sentences like 'Internships are ______ because you learn skills.' Teacher monitors and helps with spelling. Then pairs swap papers and check answers together.
pracAlt: Teacher gives each pair a set of 6 sentence strips (3 for, 3 against); students sort them into two columns on their desk and read them aloud.
Students play 'Sentence Relay': teams race to write 1 for/against reason on the board, e.g., 'You can get a job later.'
ls: Students listen to a 2-minute audio clip of two people discussing unpaid internships (KET-style). They tick 'for' or 'against' on a simple worksheet. Teacher plays audio twice; check answers as a class.
re: After break, students play 'Stand Up If...' with work-related prompts: 'Stand up if you think work is important!' 'Stand up if you want a good job!'
prod: Students write a short paragraph (4-5 sentences) with reasons for or against unpaid internships. Teacher provides sentence starters: 'I think internships are good because...' or 'I think they are bad because...'. Students share their paragraph with a partner.
rw: Students complete the final reading paper (KET-style multiple-choice questions about a short text on Labour Day) and final writing task (writing a paragraph about their ideal job). Teacher collects papers for assessment.
st: Teacher tells a simple story about a young person who gets their first job, emphasizing hard work and celebration. End with: 'Today we finished our course! Great job, everyone. Thank you for your hard work this year.'
g: Students mark off job words on a bingo card as teacher calls them out.
Students practice asking/answering 'What can you do?' and 'Why do you want this job?'
Teams stand on opposite sides of the room for/against unpaid internships and give 1 reason each.
Students say a work-related word (e.g., 'job') and the next student says a word that starts with the last letter (e.g., 'work').
Teacher acts out a job (e.g., teaching); students guess 'Are you a teacher?'
diff: Fast finishers: write 3 more sentences about why work is important.
Support: use a word bank with 5 key words (experience, skills, money, fair, learn) to write their paragraph.
hw: Review your final report card and write 1 goal for next year.
Bring a photo of your dream job to class next week.
Practice the 'job interview' roleplay with a family member.
tip: For the feedback interview, sit in a circle and use Moroccan Arabic for complex questions to ensure clarity—this respects learners' life experience while building English confidence.
checklist: I can introduce myself and give basic personal information.
I can ask and answer simple questions about daily routines.
I can understand short, simple texts on familiar topics.
I can write short, simple sentences about my life.
I can make simple transactions (e.g., buying something).
I can give reasons for my opinions (e.g., 'I like... because...').
I can participate in a short conversation about work and jobs.
